RQ2 SHAP evidence bank: importance first, direction second

Study window: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025 · Generated: 2026-07-16 19:03

Analytical hierarchy. Global tie-weighted mean |SHAP| determines which side-specific features are important enough to enter the main analysis. Conditional signed SHAP when active then explains whether those same selected features are associated with higher or lower predicted System Prices. Independently selected conditional extremes are retained only as optional tail evidence.

Model and attribution basis

Resolution Side-specific features Weighted train R² Weighted test R² Weighted test MAE Weighted test RMSE SHAP baseline (£/MWh)
Technology 37 0.367 0.509 20.16 29.18 82.4
Plant family 793 0.189 0.149 27.59 38.40 82.4

The evidence bank reads the canonical output from the existing weighted random-forest and TreeSHAP analysis; it does not refit the models. Mean absolute SHAP is averaged across the complete resolution- specific SHAP sample using Settlement Period tie weights. Conditional signed SHAP uses those same weights but averages only rows in which the binary identity-side feature is active.

SHAP method

SHAP attributes a fitted prediction to its input features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). For Settlement Period candidate row i, the random-forest prediction is represented as:

ŷi = φ0 + Σj φij,

where φ0 is the model's expected prediction and φij is feature j's contribution for that observation. Positive values move the prediction above the baseline and negative values move it below the baseline. The unnormalised SHAP values retain the units of the response variable and are therefore reported in £/MWh.

Separate weighted random-forest models are estimated for marginal technology × active side, plant family × active side and BMU × active side. Each identity-side combination is one-hot encoded before model estimation. TreeSHAP is then calculated with shap.TreeExplainer using the tree-path-dependent perturbation approach (Lundberg et al., 2020). No separate background dataset or Monte Carlo conditional- expectation sampler is supplied. Instead, unavailable-feature expectations are represented using the training-sample path frequencies stored in the fitted trees. This is computationally appropriate for the high-dimensional sparse family and BMU indicator models, but it is not identical to the Monte Carlo conditional Shapley procedure described in some electricity-price studies.

Settlement Period tie weights are used during random-forest fitting and SHAP aggregation. If an SP has m co-marginal candidate rows, each row receives weight 1/m, so every SP contributes a total weight of one. TreeSHAP values are evaluated on seeded resolution-specific subsamples—up to 10,000 rows for technology, 5,000 for plant family and 2,500 for BMU—with active examples guaranteed for leading sparse features before the remaining rows are sampled randomly.

Global importance

The primary feature ranking uses the tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP value across the full resolution-specific SHAP sample:

Ij = Σiwi|φij| / Σiwi.

This measure combines the prevalence and attribution magnitude of a feature. Absolute values remove direction, so the statistic identifies overall model importance but does not indicate whether the feature raises or lowers predicted System Price. Features are ranked by Ij, and the smallest leading set whose cumulative importance reaches at least 85% is retained for coverage analysis.

Directional interpretation

Direction is assessed only after global selection, using the tie-weighted conditional mean signed SHAP value among observations where the binary feature is active:

Dj = Σi:Xij=1wiφij / Σi:Xij=1wi.

Dj describes whether an already selected identity-side feature is associated with predictions above or below its model baseline when active. It is not used as the main importance ranking because a rarely active feature can have a large conditional mean while contributing little across the full sample. Conditional estimates supported by fewer than 10 active SHAP-sample rows are visually flagged and interpreted cautiously.

Both statistics explain the fitted model rather than the underlying market mechanism. SHAP values are model-specific associations, not causal estimates of the price effect of a technology, family or BMU. Moreover, an inactive binary feature can still receive a non-zero local SHAP value because its absence may alter a prediction; this is included in global mean |SHAP| but excluded from the active-only directional summary.

Figure 1. Cumulative global tie-weighted mean absolute SHAP after ranking side-specific features from most to least important. Markers identify the crossing feature that brings cumulative coverage to at least 85%. The crossing feature is retained, so realised coverage can slightly exceed 85%.

8 of 37Technology features reach 85% coverage

The 85% boundary is a transparent coverage device rather than a significance threshold. It provides a consistent way to compare attribution concentration as identity resolution becomes finer.
